title: Yellowstone National Park
prompt: Plan me a first-time-friendly 3-day Yellowstone trip with wildlife, geyser basins, scenic stops, and no crazy hikes. Keep the pacing realistic.
description: Geysers, two wildlife valleys and canyon rim views, moving north so the best light isn’t spent driving.

images.alt: The sun sets behind the sharp point of a snow-covered mountain; pink clouds are reflected in a pond

plan.intro: Three full sightseeing days, with arrival and departure travel outside the plan. Assumes a car and a season when the connecting park roads are accessible. Start with a night near Old Faithful or in West Yellowstone before Day 1; overnight at Canyon Village after Day 1, then Mammoth or Gardiner after Days 2 and 3. These are suggested bases, not booked lodging. The one northward lodging move protects time for Lamar Valley rather than repeated cross-park drives.

narrativeSections.heading: Access and safety
narrativeSections.markdown: Confirm [park roads, conditions and alerts](https://www.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/conditions.htm) for your travel dates before booking around this route. Seasonal closures can change the northern transfer substantially; if Lamar cannot be reached, keep wildlife viewing in an accessible area rather than forcing a long detour. Lodging and dining availability also depend on season. Stay on thermal boardwalks and designated trails. Keep at least 100 yards from bears and wolves and 25 yards from other wildlife, including bison and elk. Pack snacks, water, layers and binoculars; leave space in every day for parking and animal-related traffic delays.

title: Glacier National Park
prompt: Plan me 5 days in Glacier in mid-July with realistic pacing, scenic drives, classic viewpoints, photography, and moderate or shorter hikes.
description: Five relaxed days west to east: cedar forest, the Sun Road, east-side lakes and short photo-friendly hikes.

images.alt: Jagged peaks rise out of a forested valley and an empty road curves off into the distance.

plan.intro: Five full sightseeing days in mid-July, assuming arrival before Day 1 and departure after Day 5. Stay near West Glacier before the trip and on Night 1, then St. Mary on Nights 2–5. Cross west to east once on Day 2, rather than repeatedly driving across the park. This is a car-oriented proposal, not an assumption about booked transportation. Road access, vehicle-entry requirements, Logan Pass parking/shuttles and Many Glacier arrangements depend on the travel year and must be confirmed before booking. Mid-July can still bring alpine snow and wildlife-related trail closures; choose safe lower-elevation alternatives when needed. Hiking distances below are approximate planning estimates, not confirmation of current conditions.

narrativeSections.heading: Before you book
narrativeSections.markdown: Book the lodging split early: West Glacier for the opening night(s), then St. Mary for the east-side days. The tradeoff is one lodging move, rewarded by much less backtracking. Confirm the travel year's Going-to-the-Sun Road opening, entry rules, Logan Pass access and Many Glacier arrangements through [Glacier National Park](https://www.nps.gov/glac). If the alpine road is not open, use an outside-the-park route for the base move and substitute lower-elevation scenery; do not assume the pass will be accessible in mid-July. Carry bear spray you know how to use, layers, rain protection, water and packed lunches; follow ranger guidance and keep your distance from wildlife. Swap the east-side sightseeing days if weather favors a different photography window. Hiking destinations are described as flexible outings here; check current trail conditions before committing.

plan.parkName: Zion National Park, Bryce Canyon National Park, Capitol Reef National Park, Arches National Park, Canyonlands National Park
plan.intro: Seven travel days, assuming a morning start in Las Vegas on Day 1 and a late flight or overnight in Salt Lake City after Day 7. Follow Zion → Bryce Canyon → Capitol Reef → Arches → Canyonlands, with two nights in Springdale, one in Bryce Canyon City, one in Torrey, and two in Moab. This is a highlights trip, not an attempt to see every corner of each park. Driving ranges are approximate planning allowances, excluding sightseeing and long delays. Dates, current trail conditions, road access, shuttle schedules and entry requirements remain to be confirmed; use the required park transportation for your dates. Hiking is optional, with lighter alternatives described below.

narrativeSections.heading: Before booking
narrativeSections.markdown:
Check date-specific Zion canyon transportation, Bryce shuttle operations, Arches entry reservations and road/trail conditions before setting your schedule. Spring and fall generally suit this route best; summer calls for cooler-hour walks and more midday rest, while snow and ice can change Bryce and Highway 12 plans. Compare one-way rental costs before booking flights.

This deliberately leaves out Angels Landing, the Narrows, Delicate Arch's longer exposed hike and Canyonlands' Needles district. If Delicate Arch is essential, replace the Windows outing with that hike rather than adding it; in hot weather, move it to a cooler morning and revise the Moab days accordingly. Seven days works for highlights, but eight or nine would make room for more hiking without sacrificing rest.

narrativeSections.heading: Before you go
narrativeSections.markdown: Confirm entry reservation requirements, road access, trail conditions and shuttle service for your dates on the [Yosemite NPS website](https://www.nps.gov/yose/index.htm). Glacier Point Road is seasonal; if unavailable, replace Day 3's high-country excursion with a relaxed Valley day, a visit to the Yosemite Exploration Center and Valley View—do not substitute a strenuous hike up to Glacier Point. If the full Mirror Lake loop is not passable, the shorter out-and-back is an easier fallback, not an equivalent moderate hike. The [free Valley shuttles](https://www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/publictransportation.htm) help reduce parking moves; allow for waits and confirm the schedule. Yosemite Valley lodging best protects downtime; El Portal is an alternative if Valley lodging is unavailable, with extra daily travel. No lodging prices or availability are assumed.

plan.intro: Two full sightseeing days focused on the Window, canyon framing and dark-sky photography, assuming arrival Friday and departure Monday with a vehicle. Stay in Study Butte/Terlingua for both nights; book an additional Friday night there. Late starts and midday recovery protect energy for photography after dark. If departing Sunday, omit the second night shoot rather than rush the drive home.

narrativeSections.heading: Dates, access and photo preparation
narrativeSections.markdown:
Choose a moonless shooting window, not simply a weekend labeled “new moon”: check moonrise, moonset, cloud cover and the Milky Way core's position. Roughly March–October offers core photography opportunities, with spring often requiring pre-dawn shooting and late summer/early fall more convenient evening windows; winter favors stars rather than the bright core. Summer heat is the tradeoff for convenient nighttime timing.

Confirm [park alerts](https://www.nps.gov/bibe/index.htm), especially Chisos Basin/Window View access, for your dates. If that area is unavailable, keep Day 1's recovery schedule and substitute a permitted desert-view photo outing rather than a strenuous hike. Road access to the selected outings and night-use rules have not been confirmed. Big Bend has [no public transportation](https://www.nps.gov/bibe/planyourvisit/directions.htm); this plan assumes a vehicle, and road travel requires generous buffers.

Bring a tripod, fast wide lens, spare batteries, red headlamp, water, layers and offline/paper maps. Start around 10–15 seconds, your widest aperture and ISO 3200, then adjust for your lens and histogram. Scout in daylight, stay off road shoulders and away from cliff edges, avoid illuminating other photographers, and do not drive tired. Drones are prohibited.

narrativeSections.heading: Before you go
narrativeSections.markdown:
Acadia requires an entrance pass year-round. Cadillac Summit Road vehicle reservations are generally required from late May to mid-October; confirm the exact dates and sunrise-entry arrangements for your weekend through the [National Park Service](https://www.nps.gov/acad/index.htm). If a sunrise reservation is unavailable or the summit is unsuitable, use Ocean Path for coastal dawn instead and keep the rest of Saturday lighter. Do not substitute a strenuous pre-dawn summit hike.

Confirm road and trail conditions for your dates. The [Island Explorer](https://www.nps.gov/acad/planyourvisit/island-explorer.htm) has seasonal service and reduced fall schedules; do not assume it runs on your weekend or serves a pre-dawn outing. Pack layers, a windproof jacket, grippy footwear, a headlamp, water and picnic supplies. Foliage weekends can be busy: book lodging early, allow parking time and confirm seasonal restaurant hours.
